text.p: If business travelers find themselves lured back again and again to the same hotel, there's a reason -- the lodging industry lusts after repeat business.

The day is coming, and is already here at some hotels, when that special foam pillow or in-room fax machine the guest asked for last time will already be in the room when he or she checks in next time.

By one estimate from American Express, the best guest in any hotel will outspend others by a ratio of five-to-one. On top of that it's far cheaper to spend money getting customers to come back again than it is to try to recruit new ones.

That report was cited by Preferred Hotels & Resorts Worldwide in announcing that it had acquired master rights to Guestnet, a database that now has detailed information on the likes and dislikes of 367,487 of its guests. It will be expanded to more than 1.5 million names by the end of this year.
"Keeping customers is much more important than looking for new ones," says Pat Kennedy, president of Guestnet and owner of the La Mansion del Rio Hotel in San Antonio, Texas.

"Even with just one hotel stay a year, a repeat guest is worth four times more to a hotel than a first-time guest. Increasing the repeat guest percentage by only one point over a five-year period yields a substantial incremental revenue," he said.

In a 300-room hotel a 10 percent increase in repeat business over five years would yield $4.5 million in increased revenue, he added. And trying to satisfy those kinds of customers is going to mean "a whole new level of service and added value" for them, he said.

Peter Cass, president of Preferred, an affiliation of 103 hotels and resorts specialising in high-end business, believes the customer will see "a return to traditional service styles that existed a century ago ... where the individual guest was known and recognised."

The Guestnet computer system allows hotels to build individual profiles on favoured guests that tell at a glance how much they spent on their last visit, their hobbies, exercise preferences and any other quirks, likes and dislikes as recorded from previous visits or from questionnaires.

When the guest is returning the profile can be circulated among the hotel staff so housekeepers know if something special goes in the room and the front desk is ready with an appropriate greeting. The same information also allows the hotels to identify groups of customers who might be lured by special mail-out promotions.

Cass said business travelers account for 72 percent of Preferred's business across the board, though it runs lower in some of its resort properties. He believes that systems such as Guestnet will become pervasive in the industry in the next 10 years.

There has been ample evidence in recent years that the lodging industry needs to be more consumer-sensitive. The latest comes in a survey by J.D. Power and Associates that indicates that many guests check out miffed.
The J.D. Power survey of more than 3,500 business travelers rated more than 6,000 visits to properties at 11 upscale chains.

J.D. Power President Stephen Goodall said in an interview that the biggest surprise the survey yielded was that despite the hotel industry's emphasis on the guest, "20 percent of these frequent business travelers indicated they had experienced a problem in their most recent stay."
"That's higher than I would have thought. Also disconcerting is that only about 40 percent of those had that problem resolved -- meaning that 60 percent didn't," he said in an interview."
